scenes.display: An industrial I/O gateway that speaks MQTT out of the box.
scenes.text: Meet the IRIV IO Controller MQTT. Wire in your signals, and it publishes them. No code needed.
It reads switches, sensors and meters, and sends each one to your broker as a clean message.

segments.text: At a pump station, a float switch on input zero reports low water.
The dashboard answers over MQTT, and output zero starts the pump.
Pressure rises on the analog input, and each change is published.

scenes.display: 32 push-in terminals, Ethernet and a USB-C setup port.
scenes.text: Everything wires in at the front: two terminal blocks, Ethernet and a setup port.
Power is ten to thirty volts, with surge protection.

scenes.display: Polls Modbus RTU devices and publishes their values.
scenes.text: Isolated RS485 reads Modbus meters and sensors, and passes their values on.
Two analog inputs take zero to ten volts, or four to twenty milliamps.

scenes.display: DI0 to DI4 share the S/S0..4 common.
scenes.text: Eleven isolated inputs come in two groups. The first five share one common.

scenes.display: DI5 to DI10 share the S/S5..10 common.
scenes.text: The other six share a second, so sinking and sourcing sensors can mix.

scenes.display: DO0 to DO3, each on its own pair of terminals.
scenes.text: Four isolated outputs switch relays, lamps and valves.
One Ethernet cable carries every message to your broker.

scenes.display: The PROG port: local setup and firmware.
scenes.text: USB C is for setup and firmware updates.

scenes.display: An LED for each of the 11 inputs and 4 outputs.
scenes.text: A light for every input and output shows its state at a glance.

scenes.display: RS485 terminator, and voltage or current for each analog input.
scenes.text: Side switches set the RS485 terminator, and voltage or current for each analog input.
On a machine, it reports every cycle, and a stop the moment it happens.
Setup is a web page. Enter your broker, tick the channels, name the topics, and save.
Inside is a dual core Raspberry Pi microcontroller, in a fanless metal case.
It clips onto a standard DIN rail, next to the supply.
No scripts. No syntax errors. Just your signals, on MQTT.
Explore the terminals and compatible parts in the interactive demo, and build your own system.
